items.t: Adyen stock gains Sage role in French embedded banking rollout
sum: Adyen will provide Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure and customer onboarding for Sage's first embedded-finance implementation in France, according to a November 10, 2026 announcement by Adyen. The partnership links Adyen with Sage's accounting software for small and mid-sized businesses and gives the payments group a new route into small-business financial services.

The planned service will bring business accounts, debit cards, payments and reconciliation into Sage 50, Sage 100 and Sage Active in France. Customers are expected to make payments, manage company spending through debit cards and connect banking activity with their accounting workflows inside Sage.

Adyen's role covers the financial infrastructure and onboarding for the first French implementation. Mastercard will serve as the card-network partner for the debit-card capabilities. Sage said the service is intended to complement existing banking relationships rather than replace them.

The arrangement broadens Adyen's potential distribution beyond payment acceptance. Sage is positioning its software as a more integrated financial hub, while Adyen supplies the underlying infrastructure. The commercial opportunity will depend on the launch schedule, customer adoption and the extent of any later country rollouts.

Sage plans to expand its integrated financial-services strategy across European markets, but said provider arrangements may vary by market. The French implementation therefore confirms Adyen's role in the first market without establishing that the same arrangement will apply throughout Europe.

The next milestones are the French launch, adoption across Sage's three named products and evidence of recurring activity from accounts, cards and payment workflows. Adyen's announcement did not provide a launch date or a financial contribution from the agreement.

Adyen stock traded at 878.30 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 22:58 Berlin time on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The quote is a dated trading reference and is not accompanied here by a verified Xetra closing comparison.

Sage announced the partnership with Adyen and Mastercard on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at its Future for Partners event in Amsterdam.

According to the Adyen press release, Adyen will provide the Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure and onboarding for Sage's first implementation in France. Mastercard will support the debit-card element as the card-network partner.

The initial service is planned for Sage 50, Sage 100 and Sage Active in France. It is designed to combine business accounts, debit cards, payments and reconciliation with the accounting workflows that small businesses already use.

Sage said the offering should complement existing banking relationships rather than replace them. Customers are expected to make payments, manage company spending through debit cards and keep banking activity connected to their accounting records inside Sage.

For Adyen, the agreement adds a distribution channel beyond payment acceptance. Its infrastructure will sit inside a software platform used for financial administration, giving the company a route to small-business users through Sage. The commercial scale of the opportunity will depend on the launch timetable, customer adoption and any later country rollouts.

Sage said its provider arrangements may vary as the strategy develops across Europe. The French implementation therefore establishes Adyen's confirmed role in the first market but does not by itself secure an identical position in every later rollout.

The next operational milestones are the launch of the French service, its uptake across Sage's three named products and evidence that the embedded accounts, card services and payment workflows generate recurring activity for Adyen. The announcement did not provide a launch date or financial contribution.

Adyen stock joins HKMA group shaping agentic finance rules
sum: Adyen has joined the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Agentic Finance Expert Group, adding the Dutch payments company to a policy initiative focused on how artificial intelligence agents can participate in financial services. The HKMA announced Project SAGE and the expert group on November 2, 2026.

The membership is reported by ACN Newswire, which lists Adyen among the financial institutions in the 22-member group. The initiative brings together financial institutions, technology providers, professional services firms and academia.

According to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, SAGE stands for Securing Agentic Finance with Governance and Enablement. The programme is intended to support practical applications while establishing a governance framework for the emerging field.

The HKMA identifies potential use cases across consumer agentic commerce and everyday payments, business procurement and treasury management, and usage-based payments between machines. It also plans to examine agent identity and delegated authority, interoperability standards, legal responsibilities, governance arrangements and consumer protection.

For Adyen, the group creates a seat in discussions about the infrastructure and controls that may shape future payment ecosystems. The immediate significance is strategic rather than a disclosed earnings contribution: adoption, regulation and commercial execution will determine whether participation translates into business.

The development adds an agentic-finance angle to Adyen's recent expansion in Japan and keeps the company involved in new payment use cases beyond conventional checkout. Investors should therefore treat the membership as a positioning signal, not as evidence of a near-term revenue change.

AEX closes at 1,129.22 points as chip selloff weighs on Amsterdam
sum: The AEX ended Thursday, November 5, 2026, at 1,129.22 points, down 0.62% from Wednesday's close of 1,136.29. The decline came as technology and semiconductor stocks weakened sharply across Europe and on Wall Street. The closing level and daily performance were reported by Reuters via Investing.com.

Technology was the main source of pressure. ASML fell 6.55%, ASM International lost 6.99% and BE Semiconductor Industries dropped 7.30%, according to the closing market report. The weakness followed a broad selloff in semiconductor shares, as investors reassessed the pace and durability of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. Concerns about the effect of the US midterm-election outcome on data-centre construction and AI investment added to the sector's pressure.

The move in Amsterdam also reflected a much weaker US technology market during the European close. The Nasdaq was reported to be deep in the red, while semiconductor stocks were hit particularly hard after recent earnings and outlook statements renewed questions about demand and valuation. The AEX's technology exposure made the Dutch benchmark more vulnerable to that shift in sentiment.

Several large constituents moved against the market trend. DSM-Firmenich rose 5.49% to 113.30 euros and was the strongest AEX performer. The company benefited after UBS raised its price target following its recent quarterly results. Adyen advanced 4.51% to 892.50 euros, while Prosus gained 2.77% to 38.02 euros.

Market breadth remained negative: 55 Amsterdam-listed stocks fell, compared with 36 gainers, while 13 were unchanged. The pattern indicates that the decline was broad rather than limited to a single index heavyweight, even though the semiconductor complex accounted for much of the AEX's headline weakness.

Thursday's session leaves the Dutch benchmark exposed to developments in global technology shares and to fresh evidence about the returns expected from AI-related capital expenditure. A rotation toward more traditional sectors offered some protection, but the performance gap between chipmakers and selected defensive or consumer-oriented companies remained pronounced. The next session will show whether the selloff stabilizes or continues to dominate European equity trading.

ElevenLabs Valuation Soars to $22 Billion as CEO Sets Sights on IPO Preparations by 2028
sum: Mati Staniszewski, CEO of AI voice technology developer ElevenLabs, said at a technology event in London that the company aims to complete preparations for an initial public offering (IPO) by 2028, though the final timing of a listing has not yet been decided.

The London-based startup pushed its valuation to $22 billion (approximately NT$720 billion) in September through a secondary sale of employee shares, exactly double the $11 billion valuation from its February funding round. The transaction was sized at $300 million (approximately NT$9.9 billion), mainly intended to let employees cash out early.

ElevenLabs first made its name with AI dubbing and voice cloning, but in recent years its operational focus has shifted to enterprise voice agents, helping customers automate processes such as customer service, appointments and insurance renewals. Enterprise customers now contribute 55% of revenue, and its voice agents handle more than 15 million conversations per week, triple the level in February.

On the financial front, the company disclosed in September that its annualized recurring revenue (ARR) was about $600 million (approximately NT$20 billion), implying a valuation of roughly 37 times ARR. That same month, ElevenLabs recruited Ethan Tandowsky, a finance veteran who helped take payments company Adyen public, as chief financial officer — a move widely seen as laying groundwork for a path to the capital markets.

On the product side, the company recently launched a tool that can identify synthetic speech within real-time audio streams, targeting organizations such as government agencies that may struggle to cope with a surge in AI-agent calls. European Union transparency rules also impose disclosure obligations on certain AI interactions and deepfake content.
On the competitive front, ElevenLabs faces challenges from Alibaba's Qwen models and U.S. startup Fish Audio.
It is worth noting that as the company signals its IPO preparations, EY has pointed to signs of a recovery in the UK IPO market in 2026.

Processed volume rose 30% to 451.1 billion euros. Adyen beats Q3 revenue estimates but shares sink 10% on margin outlook cut
sum: Investing.com -- Adyen NV (AS:ADYEN) shares sank more than 10% Wednesday after the company's full-year margin outlook cut overshadowed a quarterly revenue beat.
The company reported third-quarter net revenues of €738 million, up 22% on a constant currency basis YoY, beating analyst consensus by 1%.
The payment processor's total payment volume grew 30% YoY to €451 billion, accelerating from 25% growth in the second quarter and exceeding analyst estimates of €436 billion.

The revenue growth was supported by contributions from recent acquisitions Talon.One and Orb, though the exact contribution was not disclosed. The company's take rate came in at 16 basis points, up 1% sequentially but 2% lower YoY.

However, Adyen lowered its 2026 EBITDA margin target to approximately 50% from 52%, citing accelerated investments in Talon.One and Orb teams. The company also withdrew its 2028 margin ambition of 55%. The revised EBITDA guidance sits approximately 3% below analyst consensus at the midpoint.

"While the EBITDA margin cut/waive will lead to some discussion today, we see it net positive given the commitment to topline growth and encouraging commentary on both acquired businesses," Jefferies analysts said in a note.

Adyen's Digital segment saw payment volume increase 28% YoY, with net revenue of €387 million, up 16% YoY. The company attributed growth to wallet share gains in Travel & Mobility and Content & Subscriptions verticals.

sum: Adyen has seen its share price fall sharply over the past few years, which raises a straightforward question for anyone looking at the stock today. Is the current market value properly aligned with the returns the business earns on the capital it deploys into payments infrastructure and new markets?
- Over the past 5 years the share price has declined 63.9%, which puts the spotlight firmly on whether the underlying returns on capital still justify the valuation.
- The push to scale operations and hiring in India can influence how quickly Adyen converts its investment in local payment capabilities into future returns on capital and cash generation.
- What if you looked at Adyen through its earnings instead? See why Adyen's 25.3x P/E tells a different valuation story.
For investors, the debate is whether the price you see today is appropriately supported by the returns Adyen earns on the capital it keeps putting to work in its payments platform.
If you want a broader sense of how the market prices companies on the returns they earn on capital, it can help to compare Adyen with 171 high quality undervalued stocks.

The Excess Returns model looks at how much profit Adyen can earn above its cost of equity on each euro of shareholder capital. It compares what shareholders put in with what the business can keep generating over time.

Adyen Plans Bigger Push into India, Backs Long-Term Growth
sum: Dutch payments company Adyen is expanding its business in India and hiring more staff. The company believes India's digital payments and cross-border trade market has strong long-term potential.

Adyen's Asia-Pacific president, Gary Yang, said the firm will keep growing its team in India. He did not share exact numbers for future hiring or revenue. But the trend so far is clear. Adyen's staff count in India has grown tenfold since 2023. The company had about 120 employees in the country in the first half of 2026.

India's payments market is known for strict rules. Other firms, including some major players, have had difficulties. Stripe exited India in 2024, resulting from regulatory challenges. In 2021, PayPal exited domestic payments and now focuses only on cross-border payments.

Adyen has opted for a different path. In 2024, it was given the license to operate as a payment aggregator in India for domestic and cross-border payments. The company also set up a tech hub in Bengaluru. This hub supports its operations and product work in the country.

Adyen's India numbers back its confidence. Pre-tax income from its India business more than doubled in 2025. It rose to EUR 3.18 million, up from EUR 1.45 million in 2024. Globally, Adyen posted a net income of EUR 1.06 billion in 2025.

Epos Now Turns Its POS Into Financial Operating System for Small Business
sum: The point-of-sale system sitting on a small business counter has quietly become one of the most consequential financial decisions that owner will make — not because of which card networks it accepts, but because of whether it will also lend them money, hold their deposits, and issue cards to their staff. Epos Now, the UK-headquartered cloud POS provider, has completed a five-year buildout that answers that question with a yes across all four product categories. Working with global payments platform Adyen's embedded finance platform, the company now offers merchants a single interface for payments processing, business banking, working capital, and corporate card issuing — a stack that, until recently, required four separate vendor relationships and four separate reconciliation workflows.

The timing matters. A new five-year agreement between Epos Now and Adyen, signed to mark the original partnership's milestone, extends the infrastructure bet through the early 2030s. The full embedded suite — Payments, Capital, Accounts, and Issuing — is now live in the UK with a US rollout underway; Epos Now Capital for working capital is already available across Australia, Canada, Spain, and the US.

Epos Now spent most of its history doing what most POS companies do: it sold software and hardware to small and mid-sized businesses and passed payment processing to third-party referral partners. That arrangement had a structural flaw the company has since been explicit about. By operating a referral model, Epos Now had no control over the merchant experience — cost, service quality, and the ability to build new financial products on top of the payment relationship were all out of reach.

The pivot began with payments. Once Epos Now owned the payment processing relationship, the rest of the stack became architecturally accessible. "Once payments are in place, adding accounts, cards, or capital becomes just another click," Jason Downing, Epos Now's SVP of Product Management, explained in a conversation hosted by Adyen's Carlos Hernandez at Epos Now's headquarters. That sequencing logic — payments as the foundation, then financial products surfaced contextually as a merchant's needs emerge — mirrors the playbook Toast, Square, and Shopify have used to transform their revenue structures.

items.t: Down 72% From Its Highs, Is Former Market Darling Adyen Stock Finally a Buy?
sum: Although the broader market has soared amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, many stocks that were huge winners during the COVID-19 pandemic are still faltering. There may be no better example than Adyen (OTC: ADYEY). The payments giant is down 72% from its 2021 high, severely underperforming the market.

Investors are concerned about some slowing growth and a recent executive departure. However, if you look at the company's financial performance, you'll see it has created significant long-term value. Does that make this former market darling a buy in 2026?

First, let's talk about the bad. In early 2026, Adyen revised its revenue growth outlook for the year to a range of 20% to 22%, which was below its initial projections and analyst expectations of closer to the mid-20s. The revision led to a sharp drop in the stock price.

Then, in May, Adyen's chief financial officer announced a surprise resignation. Although there was no reason to believe it was due to performance issues at the executive level, investors never like it when a key leader in a business unexpectedly departs. To pile on, Wall Street analysts downgraded Adyen stock in early June over concerns about pricing for enterprise clients in Europe.
Altogether, Adyen stock has fallen 42% year to date, with investors as pessimistic as perhaps they've ever been on this payments stock.

Adyen's goal is to have the best payment processing capabilities, both online and offline, for enterprise retail clients. That's the reason global restaurant chains and the likes of Uber and Spotify use its services to process what can amount to billions of payment transactions every year.

To expand the value it provides to these merchants, Adyen has made two acquisitions this year, of Talon One and Orb. Talon One uses software to give shoppers real-time incentives to drive more checkout volume, while Orb helps software enterprises optimize pricing and manage customer billing. Both can work in tandem to drive revenue growth for Adyen clients. Since Adyen earns a percentage of all payment volume processed through its systems, these acquisitions should accelerate revenue growth if they're properly integrated into the businesses.

PayPal's Checkout Recovery: Can Branded TPV Reaccelerate?
sum: PayPal Holdings' PYPL branded checkout recovery is becoming one of the most important questions for PYPL investors. In the first quarter of 2026, online branded checkout total payment volume (TPV) grew 2% on a currency-neutral basis, improving from 1% in the prior quarter. While that is not a full turnaround yet, it signals that PayPal's core checkout business may be stabilizing.

The company's broader results provide some support for the recovery effort. TPV reached roughly $464 billion, up 8% on a currency-neutral basis, while revenues increased 5% currency neutral. PayPal also reported stronger Venmo and enterprise payment growth, showing that demand across the platform remains healthy even as branded checkout moves more slowly.

Management is trying to reaccelerate checkout through better execution. The new operating model places Checkout Solutions & PayPal under a clearer structure, combining consumer and merchant efforts. PayPal is also investing in checkout experience, merchant presentment, consumer selection, rewards and loyalty, especially around top merchants where conversion can matter most.

The challenge is that the recovery is uneven. Management noted improvement in the United States, but Europe remains softer, with pressure in markets such as the U.K. and slower growth in Germany. Macro softness, travel weakness, local competition and PayPal's own execution gaps all appear to be weighing on momentum.

Branded TPV can reaccelerate, but likely gradually. PayPal's trusted brand, large two-sided network, Venmo integration, BNPL strength and merchant reach remain real advantages. However, investors should watch if 2% growth becomes a trend, Europe stabilizes and checkout investments improve selection and repeat usage without creating too much margin pressure.

Block XYZ, through Square and Cash App ecosystems, remains a significant competitor to PayPal in digital payments and merchant services. The company benefits from a large merchant base, integrated commerce solutions and growing consumer engagement. If PayPal's branded checkout recovery remains gradual, Block could continue strengthening its competitive position among merchants seeking streamlined payment experiences.

Adyen’s $335m Orb deal reshapes enterprise billing
sum: Adyen, the Amsterdam-listed global payments platform, has agreed to acquire Orb, an enterprise billing infrastructure provider, for $335m in a deal that aims to bring billing and payments under a single unified system for enterprise merchants.

The transaction will be structured as a reverse triangular merger, with Orb becoming an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Adyen upon completion. Adyen will fund the acquisition entirely from existing cash reserves. The co-founders of Orb have also agreed to reinvest a portion of their proceeds into newly issued Adyen ordinary shares, signalling long-term alignment with the combined business. The deal remains conditional on customary closing requirements.

Adyen intends to run Orb under an incubator model during the initial phase of the acquisition to preserve product momentum and operational continuity. The company will continue to support multi-PSP environments during this period. The longer-term strategic aim is full convergence, delivering a single infrastructure layer spanning both billing and payments for enterprise merchants.

The rationale for the deal centres on the growing structural complexity of monetisation among digital businesses, particularly as artificial intelligence accelerates the shift towards usage-based pricing models. Adyen has identified billing as a strategic entry point into a new generation of high-growth digital companies, with both existing and prospective customers already requesting this capability. By linking billing signals to Adyen’s Dynamic Identification layer, the combined system is intended to improve data models across Adyen’s product suite, while real-time payment data and risk scores will be used to optimise billing execution, reduce fraud, and improve transaction success rates.

Founded in 2021 and headquartered in San Francisco, Orb provides an infrastructure engine designed to track real-time usage data and translate complex pricing contracts for large-scale enterprises. The company raised a $25m Series B in 2024, bringing its total funding to $44m. Its client base includes Vercel, Glean, Replit, and Supabase.

items.t: 3 Stocks I Plan to Hold for the Next 20 Years
sum: Top investors like Warren Buffett consistently say their favorite stocks are ones they can hold forever. If you have a high-quality business compounding value, it is highly favorable for you and your retirement account to sit back and let the wealth pile up. $10,000 invested in a stock yielding a 20% annual return will grow to just $25,000 after five years. But if you hold that same stock for 20 years, it will be worth $383,000. That could be much more meaningful to your retirement savings.
With this in mind, here are three high-quality disruptors I believe are great holds for the next 20 years, and why investors should consider buying today.

The most important factor in finding a stock to hold for 20 years is business durability. Perhaps no brand has been more durable in entertainment over the last few decades than Nintendo (NTDOY -4.03%). The family-friendly giant focused on gaming continues to develop high-quality content and remains the leading video game console seller worldwide.

It recently launched the Nintendo Switch 2 as its new flagship gaming hardware for the next five to 10 years, and it is selling like hotcakes. Twenty million units were sold last fiscal year ending in March, with close to the same projected in its second year at retail.

Nintendo's business model works by selling gaming hardware to players at a thin profit margin, then making up the difference through high-margin game sales from first-party brands like Mario, Zelda, and Pokémon. The same playbook is being followed with the Nintendo Switch 2. Mario Kart World has sold 15 million copies, while a new Pokémon game sold 2.2 million copies within just four days after launch.

I expect the same playbook to work 20 years from now. With the stock down 54% from its highs amid fears over memory chips, Nintendo looks like a stock experiencing short-term pain that will deliver long-term gains for any investor who buys now.

No industry is perhaps more durable than healthcare. Everyone around the world needs some level of healthcare coverage, making the health insurance market a staple of the United States economy. Even if customers dislike their health insurance provider, they still have to pay premiums each and every year.

Stripe has also attracted the attention of several other venture capital investors who see promise in the company's technology. Their interest has sent the company's private market valuation soaring.

Stripe has become a leading payment processor for merchants, especially online merchants and technology companies. Its technology allows them to accept credit and debit cards, process payments from mobile wallets, and use buy now, pay later services.
Stripe takes a cut of every payment (a flat fee and a percentage of the transaction amount). The company processed $1.9 trillion in total payment volume in 2025, a 34% increase from the prior year.

The company is growing rapidly as more merchants adopt its payment processing technology, driving its private market valuation higher. Many more investors wish they could own shares of the highly valued private company.
Here's what you need to know about investing in Stripe and some alternatives to consider while awaiting its IPO.

items.t: Adyen acquires Talon.One for €750m
sum: Adyen, the global financial technology, has agreed to acquire Berlin-based loyalty and incentives platform Talon.One for a total consideration of €750m.
The deal will see Adyen purchase 100% of shares in Talon.One, a platform serving more than 300 merchants worldwide, with the acquisition to be funded entirely from Adyen’s existing cash reserves.

Talon.One co-founders Christoph Gerber and Sebastian Haas will reinvest a portion of their proceeds into newly issued Adyen ordinary shares, signalling their continued commitment to the combined business. Completion is anticipated in the second half of 2026, pending customary regulatory approvals and closing conditions.
Talon.One, founded in 2015, is projected to reach approximately €60m in annual recurring revenue by the close of this year, having expanded at a rate of 30–40% per year in recent years.

The company’s customer base has considerable overlap with Adyen’s existing merchant network. De Brauw Blackstrone Westbroek and Hengeler Mueller provided legal counsel on the transaction, with KPMG Advisory serving as financial due diligence advisor and Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE acting as financial advisor to Adyen.

The acquisition is central to Adyen’s Unified Commerce strategy, which aims to bridge online and in-store customer interactions and allow merchants to act on that data in real time. At present, merchants frequently lack a coherent view of their customers across different channels, hampering their ability to identify shoppers and convert that insight into targeted action.

By integrating Adyen’s global payments infrastructure and transaction data with Talon.One’s real-time decisioning capabilities, the combined offering will allow merchants to build a consistent customer identity across channels and apply promotions and dynamic pricing directly at the point of sale.

items.t: Airwallex is about to take on Stripe and the rest of the payments industry — in the physical world
sum: Airwallex, the Australian fintech that has spent a decade quietly building global payments infrastructure, is moving into in-person payments. The move deepens its rivalry with Stripe across the payments stack, and enables the startup to directly aim at Square and Adyen on one of the last major battlegrounds in financial technology.

Airwallex is launching a point-of-sale product that it says does something its rivals’ offerings don’t: Allow businesses to accept in-person payments in multiple countries via a single platform, without onboarding local vendors in every market.

“When a business expands into a new market, they typically have to onboard a new local acquirer, navigate fragmented compliance, and manage yet another set of vendor relationships,” CEO and co-founder Jack Zhang told TechCrunch.

In 2019, Stripe offered to acquire Airwallex for $1.2 billion, when Airwallex had just $2 million in revenue. But Zhang decided to keep building. “I even said yes to the deal,” he said, recalling the months-long negotiation. “But what really got me to change my mind is when I actually flew back to Melbourne and went deep on what motivated me to build Airwallex.”

Zhang founded Airwallex in 2015 out of frustration with the friction and expense of moving money internationally, but took a different approach than most fintech: He spent years assembling its own underlying payment rails.

Today, Airwallex, valued at $8 billion by its investors, claims it generates annualized revenue of about $1.3 billion, and that the number is growing by roughly 85% every year. The startup says it now serves more than 46,000 U.S. businesses and processes $100 billion in annual volume.

The startup currently boasts close to 90 regulatory licenses across roughly 50 markets, direct connections to local payment networks in over 120 countries, and the ability to settle transactions in more than 90 currencies. It is the very infrastructure, Zhang says, that Stripe and Square lack in meaningful ways — particularly the local banking licenses that allow funds to be held, converted, and deployed within a given market rather than immediately repatriated.

Adyen grows revenue in 2025 and targets enterprises
sum: Adyen has reported its latest results for H2 2025 and FY 2025, which saw the company grow its wallet share for customers, drive revenue growth and make significant inroads in both financial products and agentic payments. However, the company’s share price fell after its results, with reports suggesting this was due to softer than expected payments volumes in H2 2025 and a cautious growth outlook for 2026.

In H2 2025, Adyen’s net revenue rose 17% to €1.3bn ($1.5bn based on historical exchange rates over the period), driving 18% YoY growth in the company’s FY revenue to €2.4bn ($2.8bn). The company noted that net revenue rose 19% in Q4 on a constant currency basis and 15% on a reported basis, highlighting the impact of foreign currency headwinds on Adyen’s business during the period.

Total processed volume rose 12% in H2 2025 to €745bn, led by gains across the company’s Unified Commerce and Platform solutions but hampered by a 1% decline in its Digital segment. This rate of growth was slower than in H2 2024, when total processed volume rose by 22%, though Adyen said that Q4 2024 specifically was harder to compare against, given that this period saw significant wallet share gains across APAC-based online retailers.

For the full year, volume rose 8% in 2025 to €1.4tn, slower than the 33% growth reported in 2024. Having said this, the company’s profit margin has remained solid, with EBITDA margin rising to 53% in 2025 on the back of a 26% increase in EBITDA to €1.2bn.

items.t: Adyen Shares Hit Two-Year Low After Revenue Miss, Flat Adjusted Earnings Forecast
Adyen shares plummet after payments giant posts weak revenue growth outlook
sum: Dutch payments giant Adyen's stock fell as much as 20% after it posted net revenue guidance and payment processing volume that were slightly weaker than expected.
The company forecast net revenue growth of 20% to 22% for 2026, while analysts expected year-on-year growth at 22.8%, according to LSEG estimates.

"This outlook is underpinned by a strong pipeline and the continued ramp of our 2025 cohort, providing a solid foundation for the year ahead," Adyen said in its shareholder letter. "We expect market volume growth to remain broadly in line with 2025 levels, reflecting continued macroeconomic uncertainty."
Adyen processed 745.3 billion euros ($885.5 billion) in payments in the second half of the year, which came in below a 771-billion-euro revenue estimate from KBC Securities.

"Although results today and next year's outlook is largely ok, this might not be enough to turn around the very negative sentiment on the payment sector we have seen recently," KBC Securities said in a note on Thursday morning.
The stock was down 16% as of 11.15 a.m. local time, and shares are down around 16% so far this year.
Adyen reported net revenue had increased 17% YoY on a reported basis, hitting 1.27 billion euros, with both EMEA and North America growing 17% each.

Wall Street Erases $325 Billion From This Once Unstoppable Company
sum: By looking back over the past half-decade or so, investors can learn a lot about changing macroeconomic and industry forces and how they had an impact on certain businesses. There were some companies, for instance, that thrived before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. But in recent years, they have struggled mightily.
One business, which was once exhibiting unstoppable momentum, has been hit especially hard. Wall Street has erased $325 billion off its market cap in less than five years.

From its all-time high stock price in July 2021 to Feb. 5, 2026, PayPal's (PYPL +1.37%) market cap has been obliterated, going from $363 billion to $38 billion today. Consequently, shareholders have posted massive losses. The fintech stock trades 87% off its peak.

Market sentiment has clearly taken a dramatic turn, from euphoria to extreme pessimism. The optimism was understandable. Between 2019 and 2021, PayPal's total payment volume, revenue, and net income surged 76%, 43%, and 70%, respectively. Dan Schulman, CEO at the time, even projected the business would get to 1 billion users.

Then came the doom and gloom. Once the economy opened back up and consumer behavior started normalizing, PayPal's growth slowed dramatically. Revenue increased by just 4% in 2025. Transaction counts declined last year. The user base is essentially flatlining. Plus, the company just hired its second CEO in less than three years.

The biggest risk for PayPal is strikingly clear. It has to be its competition. This can be a shocking revelation to some investors, especially because this business possesses a highly regarded brand in the world of payments. What's more, as a scaled two-sided ecosystem, PayPal benefits from a network effect.

But the payments landscape could not be more crowded. Stripe, Adyen, Shopify, Global Payments' Worldpay, and Block's Square are formidable opponents on the merchant side, going head-to-head with PayPal's Braintree.

items.t: PayPal stock: 3 things it needs from the new CEO to recover
sum: Less than a year ago, then-PayPal CEO Alex Chriss boldly declared to CNBC that the fintech giant was poised to “shock the world.”
Apparently, that shock never quite materialized as anticipated – at least not in a “positive” way for investors.
In a swift and decisive move to course-correct, PayPal has announced a new leader to steer the ship: Enrique Lores, the former chief executive of HP Inc.

This leadership transition comes at a turbulent time, as PayPal stock is experiencing a meaningful decline today after reporting disappointing earnings for the holiday quarter and offering guidance that suggests weakness will persist in 2026.
The post-earnings crash has plummeted the firm’s share price to a new 52-week low, underscoring the urgency of the challenges facing the company.
To breathe new life into PYPL shares and help the fintech giant reclaim its historic glory, Lores must swiftly address the following three core issues, and that too “quickly”.
PayPal, once synonymous with online payments, is increasingly battling fierce competition that’s chipping away at its dominance.
